lesson.title: Trap Watch: False Friends in the Wild
lesson.subtitle: Mastering all 18 false friends (actualmente, embarazada, librería, éxito, asistir, recordar, sensible, sopa, realizar, lectura, delito, compromiso)

hook.title: Disarming Every False Friend on the Trail
hook.content:
Because your English-to-Spanish conversion engine is so powerful (unlocking 95%+ of Latinate cognates accurately), knowing the small handful of **False Friends** makes you bulletproof:
• **actualmente** = currently (actually = *en realidad / de hecho*)
• **embarazada** = pregnant (embarrassed = *avergonzado*)
• **la librería** = bookstore (library = *la biblioteca*)
• **el éxito** = success (exit = *la salida*)
• **asistir a** = to attend (to assist/help = *ayudar*)
• **recordar** = to remember (to record = *grabar*)
• **sensible** = sensitive (sensible = *sensato*)
• **la sopa** = soup (soap = *el jabón*)
• **realizar** = to carry out/fulfill (to realize = *darse cuenta de*)
• **la lectura** = reading (lecture = *la conferencia*)
• **el delito** = crime/offense (delight = *la delicia*)
• **el compromiso** = commitment/obligation/engagement!

pattern.title: Why False Friends Happened
pattern.content: Every false friend started as a true Latin cognate whose meaning narrowed differently in Madrid and London: Latin *exitus* meant 'outcome' (Spanish kept 'good outcome = success' as *éxito*; English kept 'way out = exit').

exercises.prompt: Match each English expression with its Spanish partner:
exercises.target_answer: actualmente, embarazada, la librería, el éxito, asistir, recordar
exercises.meaning: currently (not actually), pregnant (not embarrassed), bookstore (not lending library), success (not exit doorway), to attend (not assist/help), to remember (not record audio)
exercises.explanation: Know both what the Spanish word really means AND how to express the English look-alike!

exercises.prompt: A colleague says 'Hoy tengo un compromiso familiar y no puedo asistir'. What are they telling you?
options: Today I have a family commitment/obligation and I cannot attend
Today I had a family compromise and I cannot help
Today I am embarrassed and cannot record
exercises.target_answer: Today I have a family commitment/obligation and I cannot attend
exercises.meaning: Today I have a family commitment and cannot attend
exercises.explanation: un compromiso is a commitment/obligation (or engagement), and asistir is 'to attend'!

exercises.prompt: What is the difference between 'sensible' and 'la sopa' in Spanish?
exercises.explanation: Es una persona muy sensible = 'He/she is a very sensitive person'; la sopa está caliente = 'the soup is hot'.

exercises.prompt: Assemble: 'I want to buy the book at the bookstore'
exercises.target_answer: Quiero comprar el libro en la librería
exercises.meaning: I want to buy the book at the bookstore
exercises.explanation: You buy books at la librería (bookstore) and borrow them at la biblioteca (library)!

exercises.idea: say that you want to remember this magical night
cues: I want to remember → Quiero recordar
this (feminine) magical night → esta noche mágica
idea_parts: I want to remember → Quiero recordar
this magical night → esta noche mágica
exercises.meaning: I want to remember this magical night

summary.outcome: Spot and accurately deploy Spanish's key false friends across conversation and reading.

use_example.german: Actualmente vivo en Madrid, quiero asistir a la reunión y comprar un libro en la librería.
use_example.english: Currently I live in Madrid, I want to attend the meeting, and buy a book at the bookstore.

summary.takeaway: Always pause on actualmente (currently), librería (bookstore), éxito (success), asistir (attend), recordar (remember), and embarazada (pregnant).
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next ([3003] The Whole-Trail Review Game): celebrate completing El Puente with a grand multi-mode synthesis challenge!

twist.prompt: Assemble: 'He is a very sensitive person'
twist.explanation: la persona is always feminine (una persona muy sensible), even when referring to a man!

actualmente.etymology_derivation: Latin actuālis ('pertaining to acts/now'). Spanish narrowed it to time ('currently'); English to reality ('actually' = en realidad).

embarazada.etymology_derivation: From Portuguese/Spanish embarazar ('to encumber'). Embarrassed is avergonzado/a.

librería.context_phrase: Compré el libro en la librería.
librería.context_translation: I bought the book at the bookstore.
librería.etymology_derivation: Latin librāria ('bookstall'). La librería sells books; la biblioteca lends them.

éxito.etymology_derivation: Latin exitus ('outcome'). Spanish focused on the triumphant outcome; English on the physical doorway (la salida).

asistir.context_translation: I want to attend the meeting.
asistir.etymology_derivation: Latin assistō ('to stand by'). Spanish kept 'standing by as spectator' (asistir a); helping is ayudar.

recordar.context_translation: I want to remember the moment.
recordar.etymology_derivation: Latin recordārī ('to call back to the heart'). Recording audio is grabar.

sensible.context_translation: He is a very sensitive person.
sensible.etymology_derivation: Latin sensibilis ('feeling deeply'). The sensible, prudent person is sensato.

sopa.etymology_derivation: Germanic *supa gives English soup and Spanish sopa. Soap is el jabón.

hermano.context_phrase: Tengo un hermano y una hermana.
hermano.context_translation: I have a brother and a sister.
hermano.etymology_derivation: Latin germānus ('of the same seed/parents', English 'germane') lost its initial g- in Spanish: hermano!

cion.name: The -CIÓN Passport
cion.phonetic_rule: English -tion /-(e)ʃən/ becomes Spanish -ción /-ˈθjon/. Always stressed on the ó, and 100% feminine (la).
cion.historical_linguistics: Descends from Latin third-declension abstract nouns in -tiō (accusative -tiōnem). English borrowed thousands via French; Spanish evolved -ción directly.
cion.philological_note: Because every single -ción noun is feminine, this family hands you grammatical gender for thousands of words without memorization.

dad.name: The -DAD Quality Bridge
dad.phonetic_rule: English abstract nouns in -ty correspond to Spanish -dad /-ˈdað/. 100% feminine (la).
dad.historical_linguistics: From Latin abstract quality nouns in -tās, accusative -tātem. Spanish lenited the intervocalic dental stop to -dad.
dad.philological_note: City (ciudad), reality (realidad), university (universidad). The ending guarantees feminine gender.

mente.name: The -MENTE Adverb Engine
mente.phonetic_rule: Feminine adjective + -mente /-ˈmente/ forms adverbs corresponding to English -ly.
mente.historical_linguistics: Originates from the Latin ablative phrase [adjective] mente ('with a ... mind'). Because mens is feminine in Latin, Spanish preserves the feminine adjective stem.
mente.philological_note: Notice how Spanish preserves the feminine form: exactamente (not exactomente). If the base adjective carries a tilde, it keeps it: fácilmente.

ar_engine.name: The -ar Verb Factory
ar_engine.phonetic_rule: English Latinate nouns in -ation correspond to Spanish first-conjugation infinitives in -ar /-ˈaɾ/.
ar_engine.historical_linguistics: Latin first-conjugation verbs in -āre. English borrowed the noun form; Spanish kept the verb stem alive.
ar_engine.philological_note: The 'celebrar trap': strip the entire -ation before attaching -ar. Celebración → celebrar (not celebratar).

ico.name: The -ICO Bridge
ico.phonetic_rule: English adjectives in -ic / -ical correspond to Spanish -ico /-iko/ (masculine) / -ica (feminine). Always carries a written accent on the antepenultimate syllable.
ico.historical_linguistics: Greek -ikos passed through Latin -icus. In Spanish, these are palabras esdrújulas and must be written with a tilde.
ico.philological_note: Mágico, público, básico, económico, romántico. The tilde tells your voice exactly where to jump.

al.name: The -AL Invariable Passport
al.phonetic_rule: English adjectives ending in -al match Spanish -al /-ˈal/ with identical spelling and gender-invariable singular form.
al.historical_linguistics: Latin adjectival suffix -ālis ('pertaining to'). Both languages kept the spelling; Spanish stresses the final syllable.
al.philological_note: El plan natural, la idea natural: no gender change in the singular.

f_to_h.name: Latin F- ➔ Silent H-
f_to_h.phonetic_rule: Latin initial f- weakened into an aspiration and became completely silent h- in Spanish, while English kept the Latin f- cognate.
f_to_h.historical_linguistics: Castilian contact with Basque/Cantabrian substrate languages lacking initial /f/ caused Latin /f-/ to weaken into silent h-.
f_to_h.philological_note: Hacer ↔ fact/manufacture; hijo ↔ filial; hierro ↔ ferrous; horno ↔ furnace. When you see a silent h-, think f.

ct_to_ch.name: Latin -CT- ➔ Spanish -CH-
ct_to_ch.phonetic_rule: Latin medial -ct- palatalized into Spanish -ch- /-tʃ-, while English kept the learned Latin -ct- form.
ct_to_ch.historical_linguistics: The velar stop /k/ vocalized into a palatal glide [j] which then fused with the dental /t/ into the affricate /tʃ/.
ct_to_ch.philological_note: Noctem ➔ noche (nocturnal); lactem ➔ leche (lactose); factum ➔ hecho (fact); octō ➔ ocho (octave).

pl_cl_fl_to_ll.name: Latin PL-/CL-/FL- ➔ Spanish LL-
pl_cl_fl_to_ll.phonetic_rule: Latin initial consonant clusters pl-, cl-, fl- palatalized into Spanish ll- /ʎ/ (or /ʝ/).
pl_cl_fl_to_ll.historical_linguistics: The initial stop or fricative conditioned progressive palatalization of the liquid /l/ in Western Iberian Vulgar Latin.
pl_cl_fl_to_ll.philological_note: Clāmāre ➔ llamar (claim/clamor); clāvis ➔ llave (clef/clavicle); pluvia ➔ lluvia (pluvial); plēnus ➔ lleno (plenty).
